exercises.prompt: Both `align` and `aligned` produce a multi-line, vertically-aligned block of equations in LaTeX (both from the `amsmath` package). What's the key practical difference between them?
choices: `align` is a top-level environment that numbers each line by default; `aligned` is meant to be nested inside math delimiters (like `equation` or `$$...$$`) and produces no numbering of its own
They are exactly interchangeable in every context
`aligned` only works in text mode, never inside math delimiters
`align` requires loading `amsmath` while `aligned` does not, but they otherwise behave identically
exercises.answer: `align` is a top-level environment that numbers each line by default; `aligned` is meant to be nested inside math delimiters (like `equation` or `$$...$$`) and produces no numbering of its own
exercises.explanation: Use `align` directly when you want each line numbered; wrap `aligned` inside `equation` (or a single `$$...$$`) when you want the whole block treated — and numbered, if at all — as one unit.

exercises.prompt: Write the LaTeX source for this matrix with square brackets: $$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ Then reveal and compare.
exercises.explanation: `bmatrix` (from `amsmath`) automatically wraps the array in square brackets — compare `pmatrix` for parentheses and `vmatrix` for the single vertical bars used in determinants.

exercises.prompt: A student writes `$\left( \frac{a}{b}$`, intending to show a fraction inside an auto-sized parenthesis, but forgets to close the delimiter. What happens when this is compiled?
choices: It compiles fine — `\left(` on its own just renders a normal-sized opening parenthesis
LaTeX throws a 'Missing \right' error, because every `\left` must be paired with a matching `\right` (which can be `\right.` for an invisible delimiter if none is wanted)
It silently renders the fraction with no parenthesis at all
It compiles fine, but the parenthesis appears on the wrong side of the fraction
exercises.answer: LaTeX throws a 'Missing \right' error, because every `\left` must be paired with a matching `\right` (which can be `\right.` for an invisible delimiter if none is wanted)
exercises.explanation: `\left` and `\right` must always come in pairs — the delimiters on each side can differ, or even be invisible via `\right.`, but one can never appear without the other.
